messages.subject: Re: changing options in micro_global did not change the output temperatures
messages.subject_clean: changing options in micro_global did not change the output temperatures
messages.body_plain:
Dear Agus,

It's a little confusing but by default the microclimate model runs twice, once for the minimum shade and once for the maximum shade. This is because the idea is to provide the extremes of shade for an animal so it can model behavioural thermoregulation in a spatially implicit manner. There are thus output tables for each of the two shade levels. All you need to do is change your line:

  surftemp[k]=max(micro$soil[,3])

to

  surftemp[k]=max(micro$shadsoil[,3])

to see the output for the shade scenario.

But there are a couple of other things I would suggest. First, if you set runmoist=1 it will compute soil moisture and that results in the model working out the surface wetness. If you want to override that, set runmoist=0. I should add that point to the help for the functions.

Also, if you're only interested in one shade scenario, then just set runshade=0 and then look at micro$soil - the model will run faster as it is doing half the computation.

And, you have set the spacing quite close in the top soil nodes and your deepest node is only 80 cm. Definitely make the deep node closer to 200 cm. The deepest node is treated as boundary conditions for the soil heat balance and it simply assumes that at this depth the soil temperature is the mean annual temp. This happens at about 2 m down, but at 80 cm you will still be getting an annual cycle even though the daily cycle has damped to nothing.

I note you cut the rainfall down - setting rainmult = 0.1 means you've got 10% of the normal rainfall. Assuming that's what you meant, I'd set your code up something like this:

moist_surface=c(1,100)
maxshad=c(20,100)

# create a receiving vector
surftemp=vector()

# run scenarios
for(k in  1:length(moist_surface)){

  micro=try(micro_global(loc = c(-64.75,-15.25),
                         timeinterval=365,
                         nyears=1,
                         soiltype=6,
                         REFL= 0.1,
                         slope= 0,
                         aspect= 90,

                         DEP=c(0,1.5,2.5,5,7,10,20,30,50,200),

                         minshade= 10,
                         maxshade= maxshad[k],
                         RUF = 0.001,
                         PCTWET = moist_surface[k],
                         CMH2O = 1,
                         Usrhyt=1,

                         runmoist=0,
                         rainmult = .1,
                         runshade = 0,

                         SoilMoist_Init = c(0.4,0.4,0.4,0.4,0.4,0.4,1,1,1,1))
  )

  surftemp[k]=max(micro$soil[,3])

}
surftemp

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am working on obtaining hourly operative temperatures for various ectotherms from all over the globe over a multi year period of time. I am using the micro_ncep model to obtain my microclimate variable and I have two questions:

First, I noticed the results start at a time different from 12am, even though the time starts at minute 0. The temperatures appear to start high, then cool down with the coolest temps being in the middle of the day. So it appears that the start time is actually sometime in the middle of the day. I was wondering if there is a way to adjust for this in the parameters or if anyone knows what the exact hour is for the start of each day Here is an example of the output:

messages.subject: Re: micro_ncep hourly output questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julie

It's confusing that the TIME column starts at zero all the time, but what's happening is that the NCEP data uses Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). At your location, the local time will be different unless you're at longitude zero. Because the earth rotates 15 degrees each hour, the local time will be different by roughly longitude/15 hours compared to GMT. The 'dates' vector that is part of the micro_ncep output list can be converted to a different time zone by doing something like this:

dates <- micro$dates
attributes(dates)$tzone <- "America/Los_Angeles"

RE the air temperatures, the TALOC column is giving you the air temperature at the 'local height' which, by default, is 1 cm. At this height, yes it can get very hot. The TAREF column, the 'reference height', is at 2m. This is the air temperature we normally think of, and is what is typically used in correlative species distribution models.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Raster process
messages.body_plain:
G'day all,

Normally if I was using NicheMapR I'd set my locations of interest (often cell centroids) into a data table or data frame, one row per location, and then just loop through each location and run the model out that way, parallelizing the hell out of it if needs be. For one of the projects that I'm playing with now I've just got too many locations to model, and that approach might take me 15 months or more.

I have been learning how to use rasters as a more efficient way of analysing stuff generally, and all my data are now set up and stored as rasters, but I can't figure out a way of applying micro_global (and all things downstream) to a raster brick in a meaningful way. I figure that somebody has done this before, because I've seen some pretty big data sets produced. Anybody have any tips?

Cheers

Sean Tomlinson

messages.subject: Re: Raster process
messages.body_plain:
G'day Mike,

The high number of points is kind of unavoidable, because the focus is trying to couple edaphic data to physiological performance of strongly range-restricted plants. So these plants occur in tiny (4-45 km2) distributions on individual ridges, and even there they choose pockets on the ridges. Resolution matters in understanding where they might be, and we have pretty decent resolution in some edaphic models. We're now trying to see whether we can estimate some microclimate parameters that might make a sensible link between the local habitat and the plant physiology that we have measured at different sites.

You're right, though. If we can interpolate accurately, we don't need to calculate everything. I'll take a look at that.

Cheers

Sean

messages.subject: Re: Constant environment in two-lump
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fede,

You need to specify all the parameters for this one - that's the reason it's not working.

Incidentally, I submitted the manuscript describing this model and the onelump model yesterday - so hopefully in a few months there will be something to cite! There will be a slight change to the code for these models that will affect the results when metabolic heat is included, but for most ectotherm purposes this can be left at zero for now.

The code below should do what you want:

library(NicheMapR)
library(deSolve)

Ww_g <- 40
alpha <- 0.7

x_shell <- 0.002
geom <- 3
posture <- "n"
press <- 101325
rho_body <- 932
c_body_inner <- 3762
k_inner <- 0.502
c_body_outer <- 1313
k_outer <- 0.31

# define animal parameters - here simulating a 1000 g ellipsoid
c_body <- 3342 # specific heat of flesh, J/kg-C
q <- 0 # metabolic rate, W/m3
orient <- 1 # does the object orient toward the sun? (0,1)
shape_b <- 1/5 # shape coefficient a, -
shape_c <- 1/5 # shape coefficient b, -
shape_coefs <- c(10.4713, 0.688, 0.425, 0.85, 3.798, 0.683, 0.694, 0.743)
fatosk <- 0.4 # solar configuration factor to sky, -
fatosb <- 0.4 # solar configuration factor to substrate, -
emis <- 0.95 # emissivity of skin, -
alpha_sub <- 0.8 # substrate solar absorptivity, -
pdif <- 0.1 # proportion of solar energy that is diffuse, -

time <- seq(0, 3500, 10)
Tradf <-approxfun(time, rep(26, length(time)), rule = 2)
velf <- approxfun(time, rep(0.01, length(time)), rule = 2)
Tairf <- approxfun(time, rep(25, length(time)), rule = 2)
Zenf <- approxfun(time, rep(0, length(time)), rule = 2)
Qsolf <- approxfun(time, rep(800, length(time)), rule = 2)

Tc_init <- 0
Tsk_init <- 0
Ts_init <- 0

indata <- list(Ww_g = Ww_g, x_shell = x_shell, geom = geom, k_inner = k_inner, k_outer = k_outer, q = q, c_body_inner = c_body_inner, c_body_outer = c_body_outer, emis = emis, rho_body = rho_body, alpha = alpha, shape_coefs = shape_coefs, shape_b = shape_b, shape_c = shape_c, posture = posture, orient = orient, fatosk = fatosk, fatosb = fatosb, alpha_sub = alpha_sub, pdif = pdif, press = press)
Tbs_ode <- as.data.frame(ode(y = c(Tc_init, Tsk_init, Ts_init), times = time, func = twolump, parms = indata))
colnames(Tbs_ode) = c("time", "Tc", "Tsk", "Ts", "Tcf")

with(Tbs_ode, plot(Tc ~ time, type = 'l', ylab='Temperature, °C',xlab = 'time', ylim = c(0, 60)))
with(Tbs_ode, points(Ts ~ time, lty = 2, type = 'l', col = '1'))
with(Tbs_ode, points(Tcf ~ time, type = 'l', col = '2'))

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,

That function will just do the typical day in each month based on the 1960-1990-averaged climate dataset of New et al. 2002. If you specify multiple years it just repeats the same forcing data over multiple years, and if you specify different numbers between 12 and 365 for the 'timeinterval' parameter it will use a spline to interpolate between the monthly values. It doesn't do historical conditions. If you want that, you can use micro_ncep and specify the specific start and end date.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear NicheMapR users,

I've been playing around with the microclimate() function to predict the body temperature of intertidal mussels (Mytilus spp.).
The idea is to show that the orientation of mussels is a better predictor of body temperature than the topography of the shore.
To do so, I ran the model for all possible combinations of slope and azimuth during (i) the period I have in-situ temperature data for (2017-08-01 to 2017-09-13) and (ii) longer periods (>1 year) that will serve as a baseline for further analyses.
My research question involves two types of mussels: a dark one (albedo=0.1) and a lighter one (albedo=0.2).

The function works well for some combinations of slope and azimuth but it fails systematically under a specific range of slope and azimuth (around azimuth=280° and slope=80°) and it gets worse when the model is run for extended periods (see figure attached).
My example here is a for a site located close to Vilamoura, Portugal (longitude=-8.122935, latitude=37.070756) but I find the same pattern of failures (i.e., for azimuth>180° and slope>0°) for my nine other sites (Portugal, France and United Kingdom).

Could you help me figure out what goes wrong?

Here is my code (hourly weather data, from ECMWF's ERA5 global climate reanalysis, are attached):
​
library(NicheMapR)

path <- getwd()
load(file.path(path, "weather_ecmwf.RData"))

roughnessheight <- 0.006 # 6-cm mussels
albedo <- c(0.1, 0.2) # dark and white mussels

slo <- seq(0, 90, 10)

period <- data.frame(start=rep(NA, 3), finish=rep(NA, 3))
period[1,] <- c("2017-08-01", "2017-09-13") # my study period
period[2,] <- c("2017-01-01", "2018-01-01") # one year
period[3,] <- c("2017-01-01", "2020-01-01") # all years

results.list <- list()

for(p in seq_along(period[,1])){

  print(paste0("Running period: ", period[p,"start"], " to ", period[p,"finish"]))

  cpt <- 0
  pb <- txtProgressBar(min = 0, max = length(albedo)*length(azi)*length(slo), style = 3)

  data <- weather[which(as.POSIXct(weather$datetime, tz="Etc/GMT0")>=as.POSIXct(period[p,"start"], tz="Etc/GMT0") & as.POSIXct(weather$datetime, tz="Etc/GMT0")<as.POSIXct(period[p,"finish"], tz="Etc/GMT0")),]

  # initialization
  ystart <- as.numeric(substr(period[p,"start"], 1, 4))
  yfinish <- as.numeric(substr(period[p,"finish"], 1, 4))
  nyears <- yfinish - ystart + 1
  writecsv <- 0

  Z02 <- 0

  ZH2 <- 0

  Refhyt <- 2
  DEP <- c(0, 2.5, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200)
  Thcond <- 0.5681 # based on studies carried out on mussel flesh
  Density <- 0.001086 # based on studies carried out on mussel flesh
  SpecHeat <- 3496.3 # based on studies carried out on mussel flesh
  BulkDensity <- Density
  SatWater <- 0.95
  Elevation <- 0
  ALTT <- Elevation
  hori <- rep(0, 24)
  VIEWF <- 1 - sum(sin(hori * pi / 180)) / length(hori)
  lamb <- 0
  IUV <- 0
  PCTWET <- 0
  CMH2O <- 1
  TIMAXS <- c(1, 1, 0, 0)
  TIMINS <- c(0, 0, 1, 1)
  minshade <- 0
  maxshade <- 50
  Usrhyt <- 0.05
  relhum <- 1
  optdep.summer <- as.data.frame(rungads(longlat[2],longlat[1],relhum, 0))
  optdep.winter <- as.data.frame(rungads(longlat[2],longlat[1],relhum, 1))
  optdep <- cbind(optdep.winter[,1],rowMeans(cbind(optdep.summer[,2],optdep.winter[,2])))
  optdep <- as.data.frame(optdep)
  colnames(optdep)<-c("LAMBDA","OPTDEPTH")
  a <- lm(OPTDEPTH~poly(LAMBDA, 6, raw = TRUE),data = optdep)
  LAMBDA <- c(290, 295, 300, 305, 310, 315, 320, 330, 340, 350, 360, 370, 380, 390, 400, 420, 440, 460, 480, 500, 520, 540, 560, 580, 600, 620, 640, 660, 680, 700, 720, 740, 760, 780, 800, 820, 840, 860, 880, 900, 920, 940, 960, 980, 1000, 1020, 1080, 1100, 1120, 1140, 1160, 1180, 1200, 1220, 1240, 1260, 1280, 1300, 1320, 1380, 1400, 1420, 1440, 1460, 1480, 1500, 1540, 1580, 1600, 1620, 1640, 1660, 1700, 1720, 1780, 1800, 1860, 1900, 1950, 2000, 2020, 2050, 2100, 2120, 2150, 2200, 2260, 2300, 2320, 2350, 2380, 2400, 2420, 2450, 2490, 2500, 2600, 2700, 2800, 2900, 3000, 3100, 3200, 3300, 3400, 3500, 3600, 3700, 3800, 3900, 4000)
  TAI <- predict(a, data.frame(LAMBDA))
  TAIRhr <- data$TAVG.H
  WNhr <- data$WSPDV.H
  RHhr <- data$RHUM
  SOLRhr <- data$SRADV.H
  RAINhr <- data$PRCP.H
  CLDhr <- data$CLD.H
  ZENhr <- TAIRhr * 0 - 1
  IRDhr <- TAIRhr * 0 - 1
  CCMAXX <- aggregate(CLDhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = max)[,2]
  CCMINN <- aggregate(CLDhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = min)[,2]
  TMAXX <- aggregate(TAIRhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = max)[,2]
  TMINN <- aggregate(TAIRhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = min)[,2]
  RAINFALL <- aggregate(RAINhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = sum)[,2]
  RHMAXX <- aggregate(RHhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = max)[,2]
  RHMINN <- aggregate(RHhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = min)[,2]
  WNMAXX <- aggregate(WNhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = max)[,2]
  WNMINN <- aggregate(WNhr, by = list(data$Date), FUN = min)[,2]
  tannul <- mean(c(TMAXX, TMINN))
  tannulrun <- rep(tannul, doynum)
  MAXSHADES <- rep(maxshade, doynum)
  MINSHADES <- rep(minshade, doynum)
  SLES <- rep(SLE, doynum)
  PCTWET <- rep(PCTWET, doynum)
  PCTWET[which(RAINFALL>0)] <- 0.9 # evaporative cooling (as per Kearney et al. 2014)
  Numtyps <- 1
  Nodes <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 10, ncol = doynum)
  Nodes[1, 1:doynum] <- 10
  soilprops <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 10, ncol = 5)
  soilprops[1, 1]<-BulkDensity
  soilprops[1, 2]<-SatWater
  soilprops[1, 3]<-Thcond
  soilprops[1, 4]<-SpecHeat
  soilprops[1, 5]<-Density
  soilinit <- rep(tannul, 20)
  soiltype <- 0 # rock
  PE <- rep(CampNormTbl9_1[soiltype, 4],19)
  KS <- rep(CampNormTbl9_1[soiltype, 6],19)
  BB <- rep(CampNormTbl9_1[soiltype, 5],19)
  BD <- rep(BulkDensity, 19)
  DD <- rep(Density, 19)
  L <- rep(0, 19)
  R1 <- 0.001
  RW <- 2.5e+10
  RL <- 2e+6
  PC <- -1500
  SP <- 10
  IM <- 1e-06
  MAXCOUNT <- 500
  LAI <- rep(0, doynum)
  rainmult <- 1
  maxpool <- 10
  evenrain <- 0
  SoilMoist_Init <- rep(0.2, 10)
  moists <- matrix(nrow = 10, ncol = doynum, data = 0)
  moists[1:10,] <- SoilMoist_Init
  snowtemp <- 1.5
  snowdens <- 0.375
  densfun <- c(0.5979, 0.2178, 0.001, 0.0038)
  snowmelt <- 1
  undercatch <- 1
  rainmelt <- 0.0125
  snowcond <- 0
  intercept <- 0
  grasshade <- 0
  tides <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 24 * doynum, ncol = 3)

  # start simulations
  predictions <- NULL

  for(al in seq_along(albedo)){

    REFL <- albedo[al]
    REFLS <- rep(REFL, doynum)

    results <- cbind(data, data.frame(albedo=REFL))

    for(az in seq_along(azi)){

      azmuth <- azi[az]

      for(sl in seq_along(slo)){

        slope <- slo[sl]

        microinput <- c(doynum, RUF, ERR, Usrhyt, Refhyt, Numtyps, Z01, Z02, ZH1, ZH2, idayst, ida, HEMIS, ALAT, AMINUT, ALONG, ALMINT, ALREF, slope, azmuth, ALTT, CMH2O, microdaily, tannul, EC, VIEWF, snowtemp, snowdens, snowmelt, undercatch, rainmult, runshade, runmoist, maxpool, evenrain, snowmodel, rainmelt, writecsv, densfun, hourly, rainhourly, lamb, IUV, RW, PC, RL, SP, R1, IM, MAXCOUNT, IR, message, fail, snowcond, intercept, grasshade, solonly)
        microin <- list(microinput = microinput, tides = tides, doy = doy, SLES = SLES, DEP = DEP, Nodes = Nodes, MAXSHADES = MAXSHADES, MINSHADES = MINSHADES, TIMAXS = TIMAXS, TIMINS = TIMINS, TMAXX = TMAXX, TMINN = TMINN, RHMAXX = RHMAXX, RHMINN = RHMINN, CCMAXX = CCMAXX, CCMINN = CCMINN, WNMAXX = WNMAXX, WNMINN = WNMINN, TAIRhr = TAIRhr, RHhr = RHhr, WNhr = WNhr, CLDhr = CLDhr, SOLRhr = SOLRhr, RAINhr = RAINhr, ZENhr = ZENhr, IRDhr = IRDhr, REFLS = REFLS, PCTWET = PCTWET, soilinit = soilinit, hori = hori, TAI = TAI, soilprops = soilprops, moists = moists, RAINFALL = RAINFALL, tannulrun = tannulrun, PE = PE, KS = KS, BB = BB, BD = BD, DD = DD, L = L, LAI = LAI)
        micro <- microclimate(microin)

        dates <- data$datetime[1:nrow(micro$metout)]
        soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)
        soil <- cbind(dates, soil)

        temperatures <- soil[match(data$datetime, as.character(soil$dates)),"D0cm"]

        # keep track of failures
        runs <- rle(temperatures==0)
        myruns <- which(runs$values == TRUE & runs$lengths>=2)
        if(length(myruns)>0){
          runs.lengths.cumsum <- cumsum(runs$lengths)
          pos.ends <- runs.lengths.cumsum[myruns]
          newindex <- ifelse(myruns>1, myruns-1, 0)
          pos.starts <- runs.lengths.cumsum[newindex] + 1
          if (0 %in% newindex) pos.starts = c(1,pos.starts)
          for(pos in seq_along(pos.starts))temperatures[c(pos.starts[pos]:pos.ends[pos])] <- NA
        }

        # merge results
        results <- cbind(results, data.frame(X=temperatures))
        colnames(results)[which(colnames(results)=="X")] <- paste0("slope_", slope, "_azimuth_", azmuth)

        cpt <- cpt+1
        setTxtProgressBar(pb, cpt)

      }

    }

    predictions <- rbind(predictions, results)

  }

  results.list[[p]] <- predictions
  names(results.list)[p] <- paste0(period[p,"start"], "_", period[p,"finish"])

}

# plot results
library(fields)

empty.mat <- matrix(NA, length(azi), length(slo))
rownames(empty.mat) <- azi
colnames(empty.mat) <- slo

for(p in seq_along(results.list)){

  predictions <- results.list[[p]]
  simulations <- which(substr(colnames(predictions), 1, 5)=="slope")

  mat <- empty.mat

  for(sim in simulations){

    slope <- strsplit(colnames(predictions)[sim], split="_")[[1]][2]
    azmuth <- strsplit(colnames(predictions)[sim], split="_")[[1]][4]

    percent.discarded <- (length(which(is.na(predictions[,sim])))/length(predictions[,sim]))*100
    mat[azmuth, slope] <- percent.discarded

  }

  image.plot(mat, col=rev(grey.colors(11)), xlab="azimuth", ylab="slope", axes=FALSE, main=paste0("discarded data (%) ", names(results.list)[p]))
  axis(2, at=seq(0, 1, length.out = dim(mat)[2]), labels=as.numeric(colnames(mat)), las=1)
  axis(1, at=seq(0, 1, length.out = dim(mat)[1]), labels=as.numeric(rownames(mat)), las=2)

}
​

Thanks in advance for your help!

Best regards,

Jonathan Monsinjon

Hi Jonathan,

I just had a quick look through and it is probably because of the density you're using - it's much too low (lower than air!). That would be resulting in very high temperatures at times, I'm guessing. The units are megagrams / m3 which is the same as g / cm3, so mussels would be something close to water, i.e. a value of 1. You might want to specify different thermal properties for different layers in the soil, e.g. top 6 cm could be the properties of mussels and then rock from there down.

Note also that the roughness height isn't the height of the object, but a more abstract notion. The value you have is fine, but I just noted that you were linking it to the height of the mussels so I thought I'd better flag it.

Let me know if changing the density fixes the problem.

All the best,
Mike
